lines.text: High mountains, nomad herders and an epic longer than almost any other. This is the story of Kyrgyzstan, from the Silk Road to three revolutions.
Around the year 1000, a minaret rose over Balasagun, a Silk Road city. The Burana Tower still stands in the valley.
Kyrgyz storytellers sang the Epic of Manas, the tale of a hero and his people, one of the longest poems in the world.
In the nineteenth century the Khanate of Kokand built a fort that would grow into Bishkek, the capital.
Russia conquered the land, and in 1916 the Kyrgyz revolted. The rising was crushed, and many fled across the mountains to China.
Chinghiz Aitmatov would become the nation's great novelist, author of Jamilia and The Day Lasts More Than a Hundred Years.
Sadyr Japarov, born in 1968, would come to power after the protests of 2020, and become president.
As the Soviet Union fell apart in 1991, Kyrgyzstan became an independent country.
In 2005 protests known as the Tulip Revolution drove President Akayev from power.
Five years later another rising drove out his successor, President Bakiyev.
In 2014 Kyrgyzstan held the first World Nomad Games, with horseback contests and the sports of the steppe.
Among its mountains, Kyrgyzstan still honours the nomad life that shaped it.
